L28: ## Abstract
L29: 
L30: This document collects together into one definition all the specs that together form the current state of Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) as of 2026. The primary audience is CSS implementers, not CSS authors, as this definition includes modules by specification stability, not Web browser adoption rate.
L31: 
L32: cite17†CSS is a language for describing the rendering of structured documents (such as HTML and XML) on screen, on paper, etc.

Introduction
L83: 
L84: When the first CSS specification was published, all of CSS was contained in one document that defined CSS Level 1. CSS Level 2 was defined also by a single, multi-chapter document. However for CSS beyond Level 2, the CSS Working Group chose to adopt a modular approach, where each module defines a part of CSS, rather than to define a single monolithic specification. This breaks the specification into more manageable chunks and allows more immediate, incremental improvement to CSS.
L85: Since different CSS modules are at different levels of stability, the CSS Working Group has chosen to publish this profile to define the current scope and state of Cascading Style Sheets as of 2026.
L86: ### 1.1. What is CSS?
L87: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)
L88:     CSS is a language for writing cite63†style sheets , and is designed to describe the rendering of structured documents (such as HTML and XML) on a variety of media. CSS is used to describe the presentation of a cite64†source document , and usually does not change the underlying semantics expressed by its cite65†document language .
L89: Style sheet
L90:     A set of rules that specify the presentation of a document. Style sheets are written by an cite66†Author , and interpreted by a cite67†user agent , to present the document to the cite68†User .
L91: Source document
L92:     The document to which one or more style sheets apply. A source document’s structure and semantics are encoded using a cite65†document language (e.g., HTML, XHTML, or SVG).
L93: Author
L94:     An author is a person who writes documents and associated style sheets. An authoring tool is a cite67†user agent that generates style sheets.
L95: User
L96:     A user is a person who interacts with a user agent to view, hear, or otherwise use the document.
L97: User agent (UA)
L98:     A user agent is any program that interprets a document and its associated cite63†style sheets on behalf of a cite68†user . A cite67†user agent may display a document, read it aloud, cause it to be printed, convert it to another format, etc. For the purposes of the CSS specifications, a user agent is one that supports and interprets cite69†Cascading Style Sheets as defined in these specifications.
L99: ### 1.2. Background: The W3C Process and CSS
L100: 
L101: This section is non-normative.
L102: 
L103: In the cite70†W3C Process , a Recommendation-track document passes through three levels of stability, summarized below:
L104: 
L105: Working Draft (WD)
L106: 
L107: 
L108: This is the design phase of a W3C spec. The WG iterates the spec in response to internal and external feedback.
L109: The first official Working Draft is designated the “First Public Working Draft” (FPWD). In the CSSWG, publishing FPWD indicates that the Working Group as a whole has agreed to work on the module, roughly as scoped out and proposed in the editor’s draft.
L110: The transition to the next stage is sometimes called “Last Call Working Draft” (LCWD) phase. The CSSWG transitions Working Drafts once we have resolved all known issues, and can make no further progress without feedback from building tests and implementations.
L111: This “Last Call for Comments” sets a deadline for reporting any outstanding issues, and requires the WG to specially track and address incoming feedback. The comment-tracking document is the Disposition of Comments (DoC). It is submitted along with an updated draft for the Director’s approval, to demonstrate wide review and acceptance.
L112: Candidate Recommendation (CR)
L113:     This is the testing phase of a W3C spec. Notably, this phase is about using tests and implementations to test the specification: it is not about testing the implementations. This process often reveals more problems with the spec, and so a Candidate Recommendation will morph over time in response to implementation and testing feedback, though usually less so than during the design phase (WD).
L114: Demonstration of two correct, independent implementations of each feature is required to exit CR, so in this phase the WG builds a test suite and generates implementation reports.
L115: 
L116: The transition to the next stage is “Proposed Recommendation” (PR). During this phase the W3C Advisory Committee must approve the transition to REC.
L117: Recommendation (REC)
L118:     This is the completed state of a W3C spec and represents a maintenance phase. At this point the WG only maintains an errata document and occasionally publishes an updated edition that incorporates the errata back into the spec.
L119: An Editor’s Draft is effectively a live copy of the editors’ own working copy. It may or may not reflect Working Group consensus, and can at times be in a self-inconsistent state. (Because the publishing process at W3C is time-consuming and onerous, the cite71†Editor’s Draft is usually the best (most up-to-date) reference for a spec.
L120: Efforts are currently underway to reduce the friction of publishing, so that official drafts will be regularly up-to-date and Editor’s Drafts can return to their original function as scratch space.)
L121: ## 2. Classification of CSS Specifications
L122: 
L123: A list of all CSS modules, stable and in-progress, and their statuses can be found at the cite72†CSS Current Work page .
L124: ### 2.1. Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) — The Official Definition
L125: 
L126: This profile includes only specifications that we consider stable and for which we have enough implementation experience that we are sure of that stability.
L127: 
L128: Note: This is not intended to be a CSS Desktop Browser Profile: inclusion in this profile is based on feature stability only and not on expected use or Web browser adoption. This profile defines CSS in its most complete form.

L127: ## 6.6. Presentation attributes
L128: 
L129: Some styling properties can be specified not only in style sheets and ‘cite20†style ’ attributes, but also in presentation attributes. These are attributes whose name matches (or is similar to) a given CSS property and whose value is parsed as a value of that property. Presentation attributes contribute to the cite50†author level†drafts.csswg.org of the cascade, followed by all other author-level style sheets, and have specificity 0.
L130: Since presentation attributes are parsed as CSS values, not declarations, an cite51†!important declaration within a presentation attribute will cause it to have an cite52†invalid value . See cite53†Attribute syntax for details on how presentation attributes are parsed.
L131: Not all style properties that can affect SVG rendering have a corresponding presentation attribute. Other attributes (which happen to share the name of a style property) must not be parsed as a presentation attribute and must not affect CSS cascading and inheritance. Also, only elements in the SVG namespace support presentation attributes. Most SVG presentation attributes may be specified on any element in the SVG namespace where there is not a name clash with an existing attribute.
L132: However, the cite54†geometry properties only have equivalent presentation attributes on designated elements. Attributes of the same name on other elements must not affect CSS cascading and inheritance.
L133: Except as noted in the table for the cite55†transform presentation attributes, the presentation attribute name is the same as the property name, in lower-case letters.

L2091: ### 5.3. Cluster matching
L2092: When text contains characters such as combining marks, ideally the base character should be rendered using the same font as the mark, this assures proper placement of the mark. For this reason, the font matching algorithm for clusters is more specialized than the general case of matching a single character by itself.
L2093: For sequences containing variation selectors, which indicate the precise glyph to be used for a given character, user agents always attempt cite1301†installed font fallback to find the appropriate glyph before using the default glyph of the base character.
L2094: A sequence of codepoints containing combining mark or other modifiers is termed a grapheme cluster (see cite1302†[CSS3TEXT] and cite1303†[UAX29] for a more complete description). For a given cluster containing a base character, b and a sequence of combining characters c1, c2…, the entire cluster is matched using these steps:
L2095:   1. For each family in the font list, a face is chosen using the style selection rules defined in the previous section.
L2096:     1. If all characters in the sequence b + c1 + c2 … are completely supported by the font, select this font for the sequence.
L2097:     2. If a sequence of multiple codepoints is canonically equivalent to a single character and the font cite1304†supports that character, select this font for the sequence and use the glyph associated with the canonically equivalent character for the entire cluster.
L2098:   2. If no font was found in the font list in step 1:
L2099:     1. If c1 is a variation selector, system fallback must be used to find a font that supports the full sequence of b + c1. If no font on the system cite1304†supports the full sequence, match the single character b using the normal procedure for matching single characters and ignore the variation selector. Note: a sequence with more than one variation selector must be treated as an encoding error and the trailing selectors must be ignored. cite1241†[UNICODE] L2100:     2. L2102: ### 5.4. Character handling issues
L2103: 
L2104: CSS font matching is always performed on text runs containing Unicode characters cite1241†[UNICODE] , so documents using legacy encodings are assumed to have been transcoded before matching fonts. For fonts containing cite662†character maps for both legacy encodings and Unicode, the contents of the legacy encoding character map must have no effect on the results of the font matching process.
L2105: The font matching process does not assume that text runs are in either normalized or denormalized form (see cite1305†[CHARMOD-NORM] for more details). Fonts may only support precomposed forms and not the decomposed sequence of base character plus combining marks. Authors should always tailor their choice of fonts to their content, including whether that content contains normalized or denormalized character streams.
L2106: If a given character is a Private-Use Area Unicode codepoint, user agents must only match font families named in the cite185†font-family list that are not generic families. If none of the families named in the font-family list contain a glyph for that codepoint, user agents must display some form of missing glyph symbol for that character rather than attempting cite1301†installed font fallback for that codepoint.
